cards.title: 1.1 Representation of Quadratic Functions
body: 1.1 Representation of Quadratic Functions

**Definition:** A **Quadratic Function** is a second-degree polynomial function of the form $$f(x) = ax^2 + bx + c$$, where $$a$$, $$b$$, and $$c$$ are real numbers (constants) and the leading coefficient $$a \neq 0$$.

### Deep Dive
Quadratic functions are fundamental mathematical structures that bridge the gap between simple linear relationships and complex higher-degree curves. The term "quadratic" is derived from the Latin word "quadratus," meaning square, which points directly to the highest exponent of the independent variable, which is $$2$$. Unlike linear functions that represent constant rates of change, quadratic functions model systems with non-constant rates of change, producing curves known as parabolas. This mathematical behavior makes them indispensable for modeling physical, economic, and natural phenomena.
In practical

cards.title: Polynomial Function
body: Mathematically, the presence of the $$x^2$$ term introduces a line of symmetry. This means that for every point on one side of the vertical line of symmetry, there is a corresponding mirrored point on the other side. This symmetry is highly valued in structural engineering and architectural design, where quadratic models are utilized to design suspension bridge cables, satellite dishes, and architectural arches that distribute weight evenly.

cards.title: Polynomial Function
body: > **💡 Did You Know?**: The path of any thrown object, neglecting air resistance, is a perfect parabola modeled by a quadratic function. This physical law was first mathematically formulated by Galileo Galilei in the 17th century.

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: To easily identify if a set of discrete data points represents a quadratic relationship, check the "second differences" of the $$y$$-values for equal intervals of $$x$$. If the second differences are constant, the data is perfectly quadratic!

When a quadratic expression cannot be easily factored over the set of integers, the method of completing the square is highly reliable. This technique involves algebraically manipulating the equation to create a perfect square trinomial on one side, which can then be solved by taking square roots. Historically, this geometric process of "completing a square" area served as the foundation for modern algebraic proofs and directly led to the derivation of the universal quadratic formula: $$x = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}$$.

The coefficients $$a$$, $$b$$, and $$c$$ dictate the specific shape, position, and orientation of the curve. The leading coefficient $$a$$ is particularly crucial; it determines whether the parabola opens upward ($$a > 0$$) or downward ($$a < 0$$), which in physical terms represents situations of minimum values (like a valley) or maximum values (like the peak of a projectile path).

cards.title: Polynomial Function
body: In business, quadratic functions are routinely employed to model profit, cost, and revenue. Since revenue is calculated by multiplying price by quantity, and quantity sold often decreases linearly as price increases, the resulting revenue function is quadratic. This quadratic nature guarantees the existence of a unique vertex, which represents the optimal price point that maximizes revenue or minimizes cost, preventing businesses from relying on mere guesswork.

cards.title: Polynomial Function
body: The term under the square root in the quadratic formula, $$b^2 - 4ac$$, is called the **discriminant** (denoted by $$\Delta$$). The discriminant serves as a powerful diagnostic tool. It reveals the nature of the roots without requiring us to solve the entire equation. If $$\Delta > 0$$, there are two distinct real roots; if $$\Delta = 0$$, there is exactly one real repeated root (and the quadratic expression is a perfect square); and if $$\Delta < 0$$, the equation has no real roots, indicating that the parabola does not cross the x-axis.

cards.title: Polynomial Function
body: Understanding how to construct a quadratic function from a real-world description is a critical algebraic skill. For instance, if we consider a uniform path of width $$x$$ surrounding a rectangular garden of dimensions $$50\text{ m}$$ by $$100\text{ m}$$, the dimensions of the entire region including the path become $$(100 + 2x)\text{ m}$$ and $$(50 + 2x)\text{ m}$$. The total area function can be represented quadratically as $$A(x) = (100 + 2x)(50 + 2x) = 4x^2 + 300x + 5000$$. This clear representation allows designers and engineers to systematically calculate space allocations.

cards.title: Polynomial Function
body: Finally, when working with data points, one can determine a unique quadratic function if three distinct, non-collinear points are provided. By substituting these points into the general form $$y = ax^2 + bx + c$$, we generate a system of three linear equations with three variables ($$a$$, $$b$$, and $$c$$). Solving this system yields the exact parameters of the quadratic model, showcasing the seamless connection between linear algebra and quadratic representations.

| Coefficient | Key Structural Role | Physical/Graphical Meaning |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $$a$$ (Leading) | Determines vertical stretch/compression and direction | Opening direction, rate of curvature change |
| $$b$$ (Linear) | Affects the horizontal and vertical shift | Shift of the axis of symmetry off the y-axis |
| $$c$$ (Constant) | Determines the y-intercept | Starting value when the independent variable is zero |

cards.title: 1.2 Simplifying and Solving Quadratic Equations and Inequalities
body: 1.2 Simplifying and Solving Quadratic Equations and Inequalities

**Definition:** A **Quadratic Equation** is a mathematical statement setting a quadratic expression equal to zero, written in standard form as $$ax^2 + bx + c = 0$$ (where $$a \neq 0$$). A **Quadratic Inequality** replaces the equals sign with inequality symbols ($$<$$, $$\leq$$, $$>$$, or $$\geq$$).

### Deep Dive
Solving quadratic equations and inequalities is a cornerstone of classical algebra. There are three primary algebraic techniques used to find the roots (or solutions) of a quadratic equation: factorization, completing the square, and applying the quadratic formula. Each of these methods offers unique pedagogical and practical benefits. Factorization relies on the Null Factor Law, which states that if the product of two quantities is zero, at least one of the quantities must be zero. This requires rewriting

cards.title: Polynomial Function
body: Solving quadratic inequalities requires an understanding of intervals on the real number line. Unlike equations that yield discrete points, inequalities yield ranges of values. The boundaries of these ranges are the critical values (the roots of the corresponding quadratic equation). To determine which intervals satisfy the inequality, we can use the sign chart method or analyze the graph of the parabola. For example, if we are solving $$x^2 - x - 12 > 0$$, we factor it to $$(x - 4)(x + 3) > 0$$. The critical values are $$x = 4$$ and $$x = -3$$. Testing values in the intervals partitioned by these numbers allows us to map out the solution set.
